posts.title: Tanaka Says AI Is Accelerating — If You Don't Have AI Agents, You're Already Falling Behind
posts.excerpt: The future isn't waiting for anyone. Artificial intelligence is moving faster than most people realize.
posts.body:
The future isn't waiting for anyone.

Artificial intelligence is moving faster than most people realize. What used to take an entire team of developers, researchers, marketers, and analysts can increasingly be handled by a much smaller team working alongside AI.

And we're only getting started.

I believe we're approaching a major shift in how people build businesses, develop software, manage operations, and compete in the global economy.

My message is simple: If you're still doing everything manually while others are building with AI agents, you're putting yourself at a disadvantage.

We're Moving Beyond Chatbots

For the past few years, much of the conversation around AI has focused on chatbots.

People ask questions. AI generates answers. Someone copies the response, pastes it somewhere else, and continues working.

But that's changing.

We're entering an era of AI agents.

Unlike traditional chatbots, AI agents can be designed to execute multi-step tasks, interact with tools, analyze information, and complete workflows with varying levels of human supervision.

Imagine having an AI agent that can:

  • Research potential customers and identify opportunities.

  • Analyze competitors and market trends.

  • Help develop and test software.

  • Automate repetitive business operations.

  • Organize information and manage workflows.

  • Assist with customer support around the clock.

This isn't just about having a smarter chatbot.

It's about changing how work gets done.

The Biggest Advantage Will Be Leverage

I've always believed that building something meaningful shouldn't require doing everything manually.

As a young founder building technology from Zimbabwe, I've had to learn how to work with limited resources.

You don't always have a massive engineering team, an unlimited marketing budget, or an office full of specialists.

Sometimes, you have an idea, a computer, an internet connection, and the willingness to figure things out.

That's where AI becomes interesting.

AI gives individuals and small teams access to capabilities that previously required significantly more resources.

One developer can experiment faster. One founder can research more efficiently. A small startup can automate processes that would otherwise consume valuable hours.

But there's something important to understand:

AI doesn't automatically make you productive. Knowing how to use it effectively does.

The advantage belongs to people who can identify problems, design workflows, direct AI systems, evaluate their output, and take responsibility for the results.

People Who Ignore This Shift Risk Falling Behind

I don't believe everyone needs to become an AI engineer.

But I do believe everyone should understand how AI is changing their industry.

If you're a student, learn how AI can improve your research and learning.

If you're a developer, experiment with AI coding agents and automated testing.

If you're an entrepreneur, explore how agents can support operations, research, marketing, and customer experiences.

If you're running a business, start identifying repetitive processes that could be automated responsibly.

The goal isn't to replace your thinking with AI.

The goal is to increase what you're capable of accomplishing.

And no, simply subscribing to ChatGPT or opening an AI tool doesn't mean you're ahead.

You need to understand how to use these systems to solve real problems.

Why I'm Paying Attention to AI Agents

While building LINKUP, I've become increasingly interested in how AI can move beyond generating responses and actually help people accomplish things.

We're building around a simple idea: finding the right people to build, collaborate, and create opportunities with shouldn't be unnecessarily difficult.

I see enormous potential in combining intelligent systems, automation, and human collaboration.

And that's what makes this period so exciting.

We're not just building another generation of software.

We're rethinking what software can actually do.

My Prediction: The Next Generation of Successful Builders Will Think Differently

I don't think the future belongs exclusively to people with the biggest teams or the most expensive infrastructure.

I think it will increasingly reward people who know how to combine human creativity, technical skills, strategic thinking, and AI-powered execution.

A person who knows how to direct ten specialized AI agents could potentially accomplish work that once required a much larger operation.

Of course, agents still make mistakes. They need supervision, reliable systems, security controls, and human judgment.

But the direction is clear: the cost of experimentation is changing, and the barrier to building is getting lower.

That creates opportunities for people who are willing to adapt
